title: Investigate & ship runtime hotfix for cross‑environment GPU OOMs, KV cache corruption and memory fragmentation
creator: Marta Ruiz
description: Summary: Over the last 48 hours we received multiple escalations from Hosted and Dedicated customers (and one Private deployment) reporting sudden GPU OOMs during long-context chat workloads. Symptoms varied: (a) progressive memory growth on the device until OOM, (b) silent KV cache corruption manifesting as wrong token logits and then crashes, and (c) severe degradation in allocator fragmentation leading to inability to satisfy medium-sized allocations despite free memory. Impact: production inference latency spikes, failed user requests, and multiple emergency node restarts. Several customers reported service interruptions lasting 10–45 minutes. Triage and hypothesis: initial heap dumps and device traces point to a race in async KV eviction + snapshot/compaction path that causes stale KV references to remain in the sharded device allocator. The allocator's free-list becomes fragmented; later allocations of contiguous blocks fail even though total free memory exists. Secondary hypothesis: CUDA driver version edge-case with cuMemPool behavior exacerbates fragmentation on specific A100 firmware combos used by some Dedicated customers. Immediate mitigations applied: - Per-customer emergency rate-limiting (token-based throttles) and temporary reduction of max_batch_size. - Rolling restart of affected serving pools (hosted) and guidance notes for Dedicated/Private admins to drain and restart nodes safely. - Server-side flag to disable KV cache write-back/compaction (configurable per-deployment) while we validate fixes. Work in flight: - Repro harness: created deterministic load test using long prompts + many partial replays; reproduces growth in our stress lab with the same sequence of ops that customers sent. Test runs logged on dashboard (links below). - Fix (runtime): implement atomic eviction markers and two-phase commit for KV eviction + immediate reclaim path that releases allocator spans to a defragmentation-aware free pool. The change also adds per-stream allocation arenas to reduce cross-stream fragmentation. - Safety: add extensive invariants and ASAN/TSAN-like checks in our device allocator (in debug builds) and a non-invasive background defragmenter that coalesces free spans during low load. - Canary plan: deploy runtime-1.19-hotfix to 5% of Hosted traffic, one Dedicated customer on staging, and one Private customer with permission to test. Monitoring: added new metrics around allocator free-span-count, average contiguous free-block-size, kv-eviction-latency, and number of stale-kv-references observed. Alerting thresholds set to trigger PagerDuty if contiguous free-block-size drops below 20MB for >2 minutes. Rollback plan: if canary shows regressions (increased latency or unexpected errors), rollback runtime via A/B routing to previous model variant and disable the defragmenter; we keep the emergency flag to toggle the new kv compaction behavior. Documentation and comms: Confluence incident doc created for customers and internal postmortem. Draft status update prepared for PMs/CS to send to impacted customers. Links: - GitHub PR (fix + tests): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3124 - Canary dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/alloc/oom-frag-canary - Incident doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/ENG-9531+OOM+KV+Frag+Incident - Slack thread: #incidents-runtime message thread timestamped 2026-03-05 09:14 PST Follow-ups and acceptance criteria: - Run full 72-hour canary with synthetic long-context traffic. Acceptance = no OOMs, stable contiguous free-block-size > 50MB and zero KV corruption flags for canary nodes. - Merge PR only after 2 internal signoffs (runtime owner + allocator SME) and one backend perf review. - Add automated fuzzer test to CI that simulates concurrent evict/compact/replay patterns and must pass for two weeks on main branch. - Postmortem with RCA and customer impact timeline published within 7 days of incident closure.
